extracted.intended_audience: constitutional framers, legislators, and political theorists (educated public interested in republican constitution design)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and design principles for constructing republican constitutions and legislative structures (e.g., whether to have one assembly, two, or three branches; how to balance elites and the people). Focuses on separation of powers, representation, and institutional checks to secure liberty and justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for three powers to establish balance
rubrics_metrics.description: “A balance can never be established between two orders in society, without a third to aid the weakest.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that simple binary divisions cannot form a stable equilibrium; a third power is required to check and support the weaker order. Uses multiple analogies (waggoner metaphor, dividing forces of nature, centripetal and centrifugal forces) to show why more than two powers preserve balance and prevent anarchy or domination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of concentrating legislative, executive, and judicial authority in one assembly
rubrics_metrics.description: “A single assembly ... is to have all authority, legislative, executive, and judicial, concentrated in it. ... What is there to restrain them from making tyrannical laws, in order to execute them in a tyrannical manner?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns that a unicameral body with all powers can legislate, execute, and judge at will, creating potential tyranny. Anti-pattern: entrusting all public authority to one body without institutional checks or separate executive will likely produce oppressive and arbitrary government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep executive power separate and vested in a first magistrate with a legislative negative
rubrics_metrics.description: “To keep all the executive power entirely out of their hands; to erect a first magistrate over them, invested with the whole executive authority; to give that first magistrate a negative on the legislature ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescribes vesting executive authority in a single magistrate who can check the legislature (negative/veto) to defend both himself and the people from legislative encroachments. Guidance emphasizes insulating executive powers from capture by legislative elites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a people's house (commons) to represent and check elites, including withholding supplies
rubrics_metrics.description: “To erect on the other side of them an impregnable barrier against them, in a house of commons, fairly, fully, and adequately representing the people, who shall have the power both of negativing all their attempts ... and of withholding both from them and the crown all supplies, by which they may be paid ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates a chamber that truly represents the people and has concrete levers (veto/negation of elite attempts and control of supplies) to prevent an elite-dominated legislature or executive capture. Example: withholding supply as an effective constraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: A fixed constitution and laws known and obeyed by all are foundational
rubrics_metrics.description: “Neither liberty nor justice can be secured ... but by a fixed constitution of government, and stated laws, known and obeyed by all.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle that liberty and prosperity depend on an established constitution and clear, public laws. Implies written/settled rules rather than ad hoc or purely discretionary governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil liberty: government by equal laws of common consent, not domination by men
rubrics_metrics.description: “Civil liberty [is] the power of a civil society to govern itself, by its own discretion, or by laws of its own making, by the majority, in a collective body, or by fair representation ... Legitimate government consists only in the dominion of equal laws, made with common consent, and not in the dominion of any men over other men.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the normative goal of constitutional design: secure self-government under equal laws formed with common consent. Use this definition to evaluate institutions—those that devolve into domination by persons rather than laws fail to secure liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design must account for natural inequalities (wealth, birth, merit, family influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerates natural and social inequalities (1. inequality of wealth; 2. birth; 3. inequalities of merit, talents, reputation; 4. some who unite these advantages) that exist in every state and influence politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that wealth, lineage, talent, and family networks create durable social influence; constitutional arrangements should anticipate and manage these inequalities so they do not yield unchecked political domination. Evaluation should examine how institutions mitigate or amplify these advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid legal/artificial hereditary distinctions (titles, dignities, legal distinctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes that in Massachusetts there is 'no appearance of artificial inequalities of condition, such as hereditary dignities, titles, magistracies, or legal distinctions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a republican design criterion, avoid embedding hereditary titles or legal ranks into law, since these create entrenched privilege contrary to equality of rights and duties. Contrast with European contexts where such marks exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely solely on popular jealousy or vigilance as a check
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Will it be pretended, that the jealousy and vigilance of the people, and their power to discard them at the next election, will restrain them? Even this idea supposes a balance ... it would be found a mere delusion.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that expecting the electorate's intermittent vigilance to reliably check concentrated power is unrealistic; institutional (structural) checks are needed. Design evaluation should test whether checks are structural rather than dependent on unpredictable popular temper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent elite capture of a single assembly by designing counterweights and representative composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Without a senate or council, 'all the rich, the honorable, and meritorious will stand candidates ... and nineteen in twenty of them obtain elections. The house will be found to have all the inequalities in it, that prevailed among the people at large.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns that a unicameral legislature elected in an unequal society will be dominated by elites. Criterion: ensure institutional design (e.g., bicameralism, separate magistrate, people's house) to prevent an assembly from becoming an instrument of a natural aristocracy; examine class composition, faction dynamics, and incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect individual rights against unjust laws or majority usurpation
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Every individual has his rights, of which the nation cannot deprive him, except by violence, and an unlawful use of the general power.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design must secure individual rights against unlawful acts of the collective or legislature. Constitutions should include protections that prevent majorities from using law to unjustly dispossess individuals; evaluators should check for legal safeguards and limits on legislative power.
